claim: PSAM4-GlyR is a chloride-permeable inhibitory receptor proposed as a strategy to selectively control neuronal activity in awake, behaving animals.
source: Ultrapotent chemogenetics, including the chloride-permeable inhibitory PSAM4-GlyR receptor, were recently proposed as a powerful strategy to selectively control neuronal activity in awake, behaving animals.
evidence: The abstract directly states this as background information, citing the proposed use of PSAM4-GlyR.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR with uPSEM792 ligand enhanced rather than suppressed the activity of D1-MSNs in vivo.
source: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR with the uPSEM792 ligand enhanced rather than suppressed the activity of D1-MSNs in vivo as indicated by increased c-fos expression in D1-MSNs
evidence: The abstract presents this as a primary finding based on c-fos expression data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR enhanced D1-MSN activity in vitro as indicated by cell-attached recordings.
source: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR with the uPSEM792 ligand enhanced rather than suppressed the activity of D1-MSNs in vivo as indicated by increased c-fos expression in D1-MSNs and in vitro as indicated by cell-attached recordings from D1-MSNs in mouse brain slices.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on cell-attached recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR depolarized D1-MSNs.
source: Whole-cell recordings showed that activation of PSAM4-GlyR depolarized D1-MSNs
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding from whole-cell recordings shown in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR attenuated GABAergic inhibition of D1-MSNs.
source: Whole-cell recordings showed that activation of PSAM4-GlyR depolarized D1-MSNs, attenuated GABAergic inhibition
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding from whole-cell recordings shown in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR shifted the reversal potential of PSAM4-GlyR current to more depolarized potentials.
source: Whole-cell recordings showed that activation of PSAM4-GlyR depolarized D1-MSNs, attenuated GABAergic inhibition, and shifted the reversal potential of PSAM4-GlyR current to more depolarized potentials, perpetuating the depolarizing effect of receptor activation.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding from whole-cell recordings shown in the manuscript.

claim: DREADDs may disrupt signaling from endogenous G protein-coupled receptors when expressed at high levels.
source: However, DREADDs may disrupt signaling from endogenous G protein-coupled receptors when expressed at high levels (Saloman et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Saloman et al., 2016.

claim: CNO has been found to be metabolized peripherally to clozapine, which binds to many receptors in the brain.
source: CNO has been found to be metabolized peripherally to clozapine, which binds to many receptors in the brain, potentially resulting in off-target effects (Gomez et al., 2017; Manvich et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gomez et al., 2017 and Manvich et al., 2018.

claim: PSAM4-GlyR is a chimeric protein of a modified α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor ligand binding domain fused to the chloride-permeable glycine receptor ion pore domain.
source: The inhibitory PSAM4-GlyR is a chimeric protein of a modified α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor ligand binding domain fused to the chloride-permeable glycine receptor ion pore domain (GlyR).
evidence: This is a description of the molecular structure of PSAM4-GlyR based on established knowledge.

claim: Application of ultrapotent agonist uPSEM792 activates PSAM4-GlyR.
source: After intracranial injection and expression of a virus encoding PSAM4-GlyR, application of ultrapotent agonist (e.g., uPSEM792) activates PSAM4-GlyR
evidence: This is stated as a known property of the PSAM4-GlyR system.

claim: PSAM4-GlyR activation was expected to selectively inhibit PSAM4-GlyR-expressing neurons.
source: application of ultrapotent agonist (e.g., uPSEM792) activates PSAM4-GlyR, which in principle selectively inhibits PSAM4-GlyR-expressing neurons (Magnus et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement describes the expected function based on Magnus et al., 2019.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of uPSEM792 enhanced the expression of c-fos in PSAM4-GlyR-expressing D1-MSNs.
source: Intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of uPSEM792 enhanced the expression of the immediate early gene c-fos in PSAM4-GlyR-expressing D1-MSNs, indicative of in vivo activation rather than inhibition of these neurons.
evidence: This is presented as a finding from the in vivo experiments.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR with uPSEM792 decreased membrane resistance of D1-MSNs.
source: Using whole-cell recordings in acute brain slices, we found that activation of PSAM4-GlyR with uPSEM792 decreased membrane resistance
evidence: This is presented as a finding from whole-cell recordings.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR induced an inward current in voltage-clamp recordings.
source: Using whole-cell recordings in acute brain slices, we found that activation of PSAM4-GlyR with uPSEM792 decreased membrane resistance, induced an inward current in voltage-clamp
evidence: This is presented as a finding from voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR depolarized the membrane potential in current-clamp recordings.
source: Using whole-cell recordings in acute brain slices, we found that activation of PSAM4-GlyR with uPSEM792 decreased membrane resistance, induced an inward current in voltage-clamp, and depolarized the membrane potential in current-clamp
evidence: This is presented as a finding from current-clamp recordings.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR sometimes resulted in depolarization block.
source: depolarized the membrane potential in current-clamp, sometimes resulting in depolarization block.
evidence: This is presented as an observation from current-clamp recordings.

claim: The majority of D1-MSNs maintained action potential firing to somatic current injection after PSAM4-GlyR activation.
source: The majority of neurons maintained action potential firing to somatic current injection.
evidence: This is presented as a finding from current-clamp recordings.

claim: Cell-attached recordings at subthreshold depolarized potentials showed that activation of PSAM4-GlyR induced firing of action potentials in D1-MSNs.
source: Cell-attached recordings at subthreshold depolarized potentials also showed that activation of PSAM4-GlyR induced firing of action potentials in D1-MSNs.
evidence: This is presented as a finding from cell-attached recordings.

claim: Chloride influx via PSAM4-GlyR activation shifted its reversal potential to more positive values.
source: Further, we found that chloride influx via PSAM4-GlyR activation shifted its reversal potential to more positive values further exacerbating the depolarizing effect
evidence: This is presented as a finding from voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: PSAM4-GlyR expression was restricted to tdTomato+ neurons in prodynorphin-Cre mice crossed with Ai9 reporter mice.
source: PSAM4-GlyR expression was restricted to tdTomato+ neurons which confirmed selective Cre-dependent expression of PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The immediate early gene c-fos is commonly used as a surrogate marker for neuronal activation.
source: The immediate early gene c-fos is commonly used as a surrogate marker for neuronal activation (Chung, 2015; Cruz et al., 2015; Sheng and Greenberg, 1990; Hunt et al., 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Opioid exposure has been shown to increase the expression of c-fos and other immediate early genes in striatal neurons including D1-MSNs.
source: To avoid a potential floor effect, we treated mice with fentanyl since opioid exposure has been shown to increase the expression of c-fos and other immediate early genes in striatal neurons including D1-MSNs (Enoksson et al., 2012; Lobo et al., 2013; Chang et al., 1988; Liu et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR with i.p. uPSEM792 increased c-fos expression in D1-MSNs expressing PSAM4-GlyR.
source: Contrary to expectation, activation of PSAM4-GlyR with i.p. uPSEM792 increased c-fos expression in D1-MSNs expressing PSAM4-GlyR (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Two-way ANOVA showed a significant effect of PSAM4-GlyR activation on c-fos expression (F1, 34 = 30.55, p<0.0001).
source: Two-way ANOVA showed a significant effect of PSAM4-GlyR activation on c-fos expression (F1, 34 = 30.55, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the c-fos expression experiment.

claim: There was no difference in c-fos expression in non-transduced cells after PSAM4-GlyR activation.
source: There was no difference in c-fos expression in non-transduced cells (two-way ANOVA; PSAM4-GlyR activation effect: F1, 34 = 0.82, p=0.37; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The internal solution in whole-cell recordings contained 12.8 mM Cl− to mimic the natural reversal potential of chloride in MSNs (ECl ~ −62 mV).
source: The internal solution in these recordings was potassium-based and contained 12.8 mM Cl− to mimic the natural reversal potential of chloride in MSNs (ECl ~ −62 mV) (Misgeld et al., 1982; Bracci and Panzeri, 2006).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citations.

claim: In control neurons, 10 or 50 nM uPSEM792 had no effect on basal whole-cell current.
source: In control neurons, 10 or 50 nM uPSEM792 had no effect on basal whole-cell current (10 nM: −2.8 ± 7.7 pA, n = 6, p=0.73, paired t-test; 50 nM: −9.5 ± 9.4 pA, n = 14, p=0.24; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons, 10 nM uPSEM792 produced an inward current of −43.0 ± 10.1 pA.
source: In PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons, 10 nM uPSEM792 produced an inward current (−43.0 ± 10.1 pA, n = 21, p=0.0004, paired t-test; Figure 2A and B)
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: 50 nM uPSEM792 produced an inward current of −275.5 ± 57.1 pA in PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons.
source: Higher concentrations of uPSEM792 produced substantially larger inward currents (50 nM: −275.5 ± 57.1 pA, n = 18, p=0.0002, paired t-test
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recording data.

claim: 100 nM uPSEM792 produced an inward current of −410.1 ± 137.8 pA in PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons.
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The basal membrane resistance of D1-MSNs was 78.6 ± 5.5 MΩ.
source: The basal membrane resistance of D1-MSNs was 78.6 ± 5.5 MΩ, consistent with a previous report using similar recording conditions (Planert et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a measurement from voltage-clamp recordings, consistent with a cited previous report.

claim: 50 nM uPSEM792 decreased membrane resistance by 29.6 ± 5.3% in PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons.
source: and was reduced by activation of PSAM4-GlyR (10 nM: 6.5 ± 3.3% decrease, n = 9, p=0.08, paired t-test; 50 nM: 29.6 ± 5.3% decrease, n = 18, p<0.0001; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PSAM4-GlyR activation by uPSEM792 significantly depolarized the membrane potential of PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons compared to control neurons.
source: PSAM4-GlyR activation by uPSEM792 significantly depolarized the membrane potential of PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons compared to control neurons (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by current-clamp recording data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Two-way ANOVA showed a significant effect of PSAM4-GlyR activation on membrane potential (F1, 37 = 9.70, p=0.004).
source: Two-way ANOVA showed a significant effect of PSAM4-GlyR activation on membrane potential (F1, 37 = 9.70, p=0.004)
evidence: This is a statistical result from current-clamp recordings.

claim: The resting membrane potential of D1-MSNs was −83.3 ± 0.7 mV.
source: Relative to the resting membrane potential (−83.3 ± 0.7 mV), the depolarization induced by 10 and 50 nM uPSEM792 was 6.4 ± 2.0 mV (n = 14, p=0.007, paired t-test) and 20.9 ± 3.4 mV (n = 16, p<0.0001), respectively.
evidence: This is a measurement from current-clamp recordings.

claim: 10 nM uPSEM792 induced a depolarization of 6.4 ± 2.0 mV in PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons.
source: Relative to the resting membrane potential (−83.3 ± 0.7 mV), the depolarization induced by 10 and 50 nM uPSEM792 was 6.4 ± 2.0 mV (n = 14, p=0.007, paired t-test)
evidence: This is a measurement from current-clamp recordings.

claim: 50 nM uPSEM792 induced a depolarization of 20.9 ± 3.4 mV in PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons.
source: the depolarization induced by 10 and 50 nM uPSEM792 was 6.4 ± 2.0 mV (n = 14, p=0.007, paired t-test) and 20.9 ± 3.4 mV (n = 16, p<0.0001), respectively.
evidence: This is a measurement from current-clamp recordings.

claim: In 10 nM uPSEM792, 14/14 PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons continued to fire with current injection.
source: In PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons, all neurons treated with 10 nM uPSEM792 continued to fire action potentials with somatic current injections (n = 14, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by current-clamp recording data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In 50 nM uPSEM792, 10 of 16 PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons continued to fire action potentials with current injection.
source: In 50 nM uPSEM792, 10 of 16 neurons continued to fire action potentials with current injection
evidence: This is supported by current-clamp recording data.

claim: In 50 nM uPSEM792, 6 of 16 PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons were depolarized sufficiently to enter into depolarization block.
source: In 50 nM uPSEM792, 10 of 16 neurons continued to fire action potentials with current injection and 6 of 16 neurons were depolarized sufficiently to enter into depolarization block upon uPSEM792 application (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by current-clamp recording data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Neurons that entered into depolarization block had higher membrane resistance (92.4 ± 5.2 mΩ) compared to neurons that continued to fire (65.8 ± 6.7 mΩ).
source: When compared with neurons that continued to fire, neurons that entered into depolarization block with uPSEM792 application had similar resting membrane potential to other PSAM4-GlyR neurons (−83.1 ± 1.1 mV vs. −83.6 ± 1.3 mV), but had higher membrane resistance (92.4 ± 5.2 mΩ vs. 65.8 ± 6.7 mΩ)
evidence: This is a comparison of electrophysiological properties between two groups of neurons.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs did not suppress high-potassium-induced firing of action potentials in cell-attached recordings.
source: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs did not suppress high-potassium-induced firing of action potentials (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recording data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: In one of five neurons, activation of PSAM4-GlyR induced firing prior to high potassium application in cell-attached recordings.
source: In fact, in one of five neurons, activation of PSAM4-GlyR induced firing prior to high potassium application (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from cell-attached recordings.

claim: Cell-attached recordings show that activation of PSAM4-GlyR triggered firing of D1 MSNs when neurons were depolarized to subthreshold potentials by increasing extracellular potassium.
source: Under these conditions, cell-attached recordings show that activation of PSAM4-GlyR triggered firing of D1 MSNs (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recording data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: In control cells, uPSEM792 did not result in firing in cell-attached recordings with elevated extracellular potassium.
source: In control cells, uPSEM792 did not result in firing, unlike high potassium application (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by cell-attached recording data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: A mixed-effects two-way ANOVA showed a significant interaction effect between PSAM4-GlyR expression and recording condition on the firing frequency (F2, 13 = 12.40, p=0.001).
source: A mixed-effects two-way ANOVA showed a significant interaction effect between PSAM4-GlyR expression (+ vs. −) and recording condition (aCSF vs. uPSEM vs. high potassium) on the firing frequency (F2, 13 = 12.40, p=0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from cell-attached recordings.

claim: The transient PSAM4-GlyR current reversed polarity at −61.4 mV.
source: The transient current reversed polarity at −61.4 mV (n = 21, CI: −64.0 to −59.0 mV, linear regression, r2 = 0.58, F1, 103 = 142.5, p<0.0001), consistent with the calculated reversal potential of the PSAM4-GlyR channel.
evidence: This is a measurement from voltage-clamp recordings using voltage steps.

claim: At steady state, the reversal potential of PSAM4-GlyR current showed a significant rightward shift to −44.2 mV.
source: At steady state, the reversal potential of PSAM4-GlyR current showed a significant rightward shift to −44.2 mV (n = 21, CI: −48.3 to −38.2 mV, linear regression, r2 = 0.39, F1, 103 = 66.9, p<0.0001; paired t-test, t = 5.73, p<0.0001, Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is a measurement from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The steady-state current showed a U-shaped current–voltage relationship.
source: Further, the steady-state current showed a U-shaped current–voltage relationship (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is an observation from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The steady-state outward current component was significantly smaller than the transient outward current (49.8 ± 38.4 pA vs. 307.1 ± 62.0 pA at Vhold −28 mV).
source: the outward current component was significantly smaller than the transient outward current (49.8 ± 38.4 pA vs. 307.1 ± 62.0 pA at Vhold −28 mV respectively, unpaired t-test, p<0.0001; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a comparison of current measurements from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The magnitude of the tail current increased substantially with preceding depolarizing steps.
source: Further, the magnitude of the tail current increased substantially with preceding depolarizing steps (Figure 5F and G; RM two-way ANOVA, significant PSAM4-GlyR activation effect: F1, 30 = 18.05, p=0.0002; significant PSAM4-GlyR activation × voltage step interaction: F9, 270 = 9.55, p<0.0001
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The magnitude of the shift in reversal potential was positively correlated with the conductance of PSAM4-GlyR (Pearson's correlation, r = 0.57, p=0.0008, n = 21).
source: In addition, the magnitude of the shift in reversal potential was positively correlated with the conductance of PSAM4-GlyR, measured at Vhold −88 mV (Pearson's correlation, r = 0.57, p=0.0008, n = 21; Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis of voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Sustained activation of chloride conductances including GABAA receptors can lead to chloride influx that overwhelms homeostatic mechanisms to pump chloride out.
source: Indeed, many reports show that sustained activation of chloride conductances including GABAA receptors (Huguenard and Alger, 1986; Staley et al., 1995; Thompson and Gähwiler, 1989), glycine receptors (Karlsson et al., 2011), and Halorhodopsin (Raimondo et al., 2012; Alfonsa et al., 2015) can lead to chloride influx that overwhelms homeostatic mechanisms to pump chloride out, thereby elevating the intracellular chloride concentration.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Shifts in intracellular chloride concentration have been shown to result in 'apparent cross-desensitization' of glycine- and GABAA receptors.
source: Shifts in intracellular chloride concentration have been shown to result in 'apparent cross-desensitization' of glycine- and GABAA receptors whereby sustained activation of one chloride-permeable channel (e.g., glycine channel) results in reduced currents carried by another chloride-permeable channel (e.g., GABAA channel) and vice versa (Karlsson et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Karlsson et al., 2011.

claim: In neurons that showed a rightward shift in reversal potential of PSAM4-GlyR (>5 mV shift), the amplitude of the GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic currents significantly decreased upon activation of PSAM4-GlyR.
source: In neurons that showed a rightward shift in reversal potential of PSAM4-GlyR (>5 mV shift, n = 5, Erevshift = 17.3 ± 6.3 mV), the amplitude of the GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic currents significantly decreased upon activation of PSAM4-GlyR compared with aCSF (−33.4 ± 6.0 pA vs. −7.8 ± 1.3 pA at Vhold −88 mV, paired t-test: p=0.01; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The reversal potential of GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic currents showed a significant rightward shift from −60.9 mV in aCSF to −51.6 mV upon activation of PSAM4-GlyR in neurons with >5 mV shift in PSAM4-GlyR reversal potential.
source: Further, the reversal potential of GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic currents showed a significant rightward shift from −60.9 mV in aCSF to −51.6 mV upon activation of PSAM4-GlyR (aCSF: CI: −64.2 to −58.1 mV, linear regression, r2 = 0.78, F1, 13 = 43.7, p<0.0001; uPSEM792: CI: −55.2 to −46.7 mV, r2 = 0.66, F1, 7 = 13.7, p=0.008; test of equal intercepts: F1, 21 = 18.3, p=0.0003; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In neurons that did not show a shift in reversal potential of PSAM4-GlyR, there was no change in the reversal potential or amplitude of GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic currents.
source: In neurons that did not show a shift in reversal potential of PSAM4-GlyR (n = 3, Erevshift = 2.1 ± 1.0 mV), there was no change in the reversal potential or amplitude of GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic currents (aCSF: GABAAErev = −64.7 mV, CI: −68.5 to −62.1 mV, linear regression, r2 = 0.91, F1, 7 = 68.8, p<0.0001; uPSEM792: GABAAErev = −64.9 mV, CI: −66.7 to −63.4 mV, r2 = 0.96, F1, 4 = 87.5, p=0.0007; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp recording data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Activation of PSAM4-GlyR reduced GABAergic inhibition of D1-MSNs.
source: These results indicate that activation of PSAM4-GlyR reduced GABAergic inhibition of D1-MSNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GABAA receptor synaptic current data.

claim: Engineered receptors to promote excitation have been largely successful.
source: Engineered receptors to promote excitation (e.g., Channelrhodopsin-2, Gq-DREADDs) have been largely successful, albeit with careful consideration of ligand-related off-target effects (Gomez et al., 2017; Manvich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by citations.

claim: Silencing of neuronal firing has been uniquely challenging, especially when relying on chloride conductances.
source: In contrast, silencing of neuronal firing has been uniquely challenging, especially when relying on chloride conductances (Wiegert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by a citation.

claim: The utility of a chloride conductance like PSAM4-GlyR to silence firing relies on hyperpolarization of the membrane at potentials more positive than the chloride reversal potential and/or the efficacy of the channels to shunt membrane depolarization.
source: The utility of a chloride conductance like PSAM4-GlyR to silence firing relies on hyperpolarization of the membrane at potentials more positive than the chloride reversal potential and/or the efficacy of the channels to shunt membrane depolarization (Doyon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about chloride conductances supported by a citation.

claim: PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs is predominantly depolarizing.
source: The present study shows that PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs is predominantly depolarizing
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: PSAM4-GlyR fails to inhibit neuronal firing in D1-MSNs.
source: The present study shows that PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs is predominantly depolarizing, fails to inhibit neuronal firing
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: PSAM4-GlyR triggers action potential firing when neurons are depolarized to subthreshold potentials.
source: The present study shows that PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs is predominantly depolarizing, fails to inhibit neuronal firing, triggers action potential firing when neurons are depolarized to subthreshold potentials
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: PSAM4-GlyR has a limited capacity to hyperpolarize D1-MSNs even at more depolarized potentials.
source: The present study shows that PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs is predominantly depolarizing, fails to inhibit neuronal firing, triggers action potential firing when neurons are depolarized to subthreshold potentials, and has a limited capacity to hyperpolarize these neurons even at more depolarized potentials.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: When activated near the resting membrane potential (−83 mV), PSAM4-GlyR passes inward current and depolarizes D1-MSNs.
source: When activated near the resting membrane potential (−83 mV), PSAM4-GlyR passes inward current and depolarizes D1-MSNs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from voltage-clamp and current-clamp recordings.

claim: When activated at potentials more depolarized than the chloride reversal potential, PSAM4-GlyR passes transient or small outward currents.
source: When activated at potentials more depolarized than the chloride reversal potential, PSAM4-GlyR passes transient or small outward currents, likely due to influx and accumulation of intracellular chloride that overwhelms endogenous mechanisms to restore the chloride gradient (Huguenard and Alger, 1986; Staley et al., 1995; Thompson and Gähwiler, 1989; Karlsson et al., 2011; Raimondo et al., 2012; Alfonsa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from voltage-clamp recordings, with mechanistic interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The release and clearance of endogenous neurotransmitters are usually tightly controlled and occur over the scale of milliseconds.
source: The release and clearance of endogenous neurotransmitters are usually tightly controlled and occur over the scale of milliseconds, allowing the neurons to better maintain a stable intra- and extracellular chloride gradient.
evidence: This is a statement about neurotransmitter dynamics based on established knowledge.

claim: Exogenous agonists result in sustained activation over seconds or minutes and cause massive chloride influx and a shift in chloride reversal potential.
source: This is unlike exogenous agonists that result in sustained activation over seconds or minutes and cause massive chloride influx and a shift in chloride reversal potential.
evidence: This is a comparison between endogenous and exogenous activation, based on the study's findings and general knowledge.

claim: While there was a significant decrease in membrane resistance associated with opening PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs (~30% reduction), it was not sufficient to prevent suprathreshold depolarization by current injection.
source: While there was a significant decrease in membrane resistance associated with opening PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs (~30% reduction), it was not sufficient to prevent suprathreshold depolarization by current injection.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from current-clamp recordings.

claim: The decrease in membrane resistance observed was lower than previously reported in cortical layer 2/3 neurons where PSAM4-GlyR activation suppressed firing.
source: Despite using high viral titer in our experiments, the decrease in membrane resistance we observed was lower than previously reported in cortical layer 2/3 neurons where PSAM4-GlyR activation suppressed firing (Magnus et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study cited.

claim: The data show a strong correlation between PSAM4-GlyR conductance and the rightward shift in PSAM4-GlyR reversal potential.
source: the data in this study show a strong correlation between PSAM4-GlyR conductance and the rightward shift in PSAM4-GlyR reversal potential, suggesting that increasing expression levels will only promote further depolarization with PSAM4-GlyR activation.
evidence: This refers to the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The lack of shunting efficacy in D1-MSNs is likely due to their low membrane resistance (~78 MΩ in brain slices) relative to other neurons in the brain.
source: The lack of shunting efficacy in D1-MSNs is likely due to their low membrane resistance (~78 MΩ in brain slices as measured above) relative to other neurons in the brain (e.g., pyramidal neurons in cortex and hippocampus).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on comparison with other neuron types.

claim: Membrane resistance is inversely proportional to temperature, age, and number/activity of synaptic inputs.
source: It is important to note that membrane resistance is inversely proportional to temperature, age, and number/activity of synaptic inputs (Kroon et al., 2019; Waters and Helmchen, 2006; Fernandez et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The shunting efficacy of PSAM4-GlyRs during behavioral experiments in vivo is likely to be lower than in brain slices.
source: and therefore, the shunting efficacy of PSAM4-GlyRs during behavioral experiments in vivo is likely to be lower than in brain slices.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between membrane resistance and experimental conditions.

claim: In the awake behaving state in vivo, MSNs show brief and irregular spontaneous membrane potential fluctuations between depolarizations (−50 to −60 mV) and hyperpolarizations (−80 to −90 mV), with the overall membrane potential following a Gaussian distribution (mean ~ −69 mV).
source: In the awake behaving state in vivo, MSNs show brief and irregular spontaneous membrane potential fluctuations between depolarizations (−50 to −60 mV) that facilitate action potential firing and hyperpolarizations (−80 to −90 mV), with the overall membrane potential following a Gaussian distribution (mean ~ −69 mV) (Mahon et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mahon et al., 2006.

claim: PSAM4-GlyR activation will effectively increase the probability and duration of spontaneous depolarizations in vivo.
source: This implies that in vivo, PSAM4-GlyR activation will effectively increase the probability and duration of spontaneous depolarizations, and increase the probability of D1-MSN firing especially during these depolarizations.
